newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SHARP FALL IN CRUDE PRICES HELPS S.AFRICA JUNE PPI.
newsitem.headline: SHARP FALL IN CRUDE PRICES HELPS S.AFRICA JUNE PPI.

text.p: A sharp fall in imported crude petroleum prices was behind the surprise drop in month-on-month producer inflation in June, economists said on Tuesday.

The Central Statistical Service (CSS) earlier reported the producer price index decreased by 0.2 percent in June after rising 0.9 percent in May giving a 7.5 percent year-on-year increase from 8.4 percent previously.
Reuters' consensus poll of 10 economists called for a 0.5 percent month-on-month and 8.3 percent year-on-year rise from a range of 7.8 to 8.5 percent.

"The sharp fall in crude oil was obviously a major factor," said Barnard Jacobs Mellet economist Chantal Friedman, whose forecast of a 7.8 percent year-on-year rise was the closest to the actual figure.
CSS said imported inflation fell by 1.4 percent month-on-month, mainly as a result of a 9.5 percent drop in the average price of imported crude.
It said the actual information received from Customs and Excise, which supplies CSS with crude oil price changes, reflected a decrease of 18.9 percent.
"However, Customs and Excise also reported that a number of crude petroleum consignments worth approximately one billion rand still have to be cleared at the Cape Town Harbour.

"Due to this lack of information for June 1997, the CSS used the average prices of May 1997 and June 1997 to calculate an average price for June 1997, which then reflects a decrease of 9.5 percent," it said.

"The 9.5 percent just reflects that there was an over-estimation of rand crude prices at the beginning of May and we are now probably back on track," said E.W. Balderson economist Mike Schussler, noting that sharply higher crude prices were the main reason for the 2.7 percent month-on-month increase in imported inflation in May.
"With this type of figure we could expect PPI back around the five percent level by year-end," Schussler added.
Friedman noted that the latest data meant that the average monthly increase in the first six months of the year was 0.4 percent.

"That is half of the 0.8 percent increase recorded in the second half of last year, so the trend is definitely downwards and we could well be looking at a year-end figure of six percent," Friedman said.
